text: Explainability asks why the model said that. Fairness asks a harder question: who bears the mistakes? A model can be accurate on average and still treat groups very differently.

Bias is rarely a bug in the algorithm. It enters through history, when the data reflects past unequal treatment. Through labels that are a biased stand-in for the truth. Through proxy features that quietly encode the group. And through how a score is used, in a setting it was never built for.

The key habit is to never report one overall number. Slice the metrics by group: the selection rate, the true positive rate, the false positive rate, and precision. Here is a synthetic loan model, trained without the group column at all.

It approves sixty-four percent of group A, but only twenty-seven percent of group B. An impact ratio of point four one five. The group was never a feature, yet the gap appeared, because income and credit history act as proxies. Notice precision is nearly equal, while the true positive rate is not.
A simple chart makes the gap easy to show to a non-technical reviewer. Same model, same cutoff, very different outcomes by group.

Can we fix it with a different cutoff per group? Equalize selection, and the true positive and false positive rates are no longer equal. Equalize the true positive rate, and selection and precision are still unequal. Fix one metric, and others move, because the groups have different base rates.

So fairness is a judgment, made in the open. Report by group with sample sizes. Decide which error matters most, with legal and domain input. Document the trade-off. And monitor after launch, with a way to appeal decisions.
